title: Four Adjectives That Do Not Agree

lessons.title: आसान / मुश्किल (āsān / mushkil) — easy, difficult, and two words that refuse to agree
lessons.gloss: easy and difficult — two loanwords, and neither of them bends

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: You know that काला changes its ending to match the noun and सफ़ेद never does. Before reading on: which of those two do you expect a word borrowed from Persian to behave like?

blocks.title: You'll want to know: आसान and मुश्किल

segments.text: Both are borrowed, and both behave like सफ़ेद: they sit in front of the noun and do not change ending for anything. Whatever the noun's gender or number, the adjective is the same shape you learned.
आसान comes from Persian āsān, "easy" — a plain everyday word in both languages, with no complication to report, which is fitting.

मुश्किल is the more interesting half. It is Arabic mushkil, from the root ش-ك-ل (sh-k-l), which is about form and shape. A mushkil thing is one whose shape is unclear — something you cannot make out the outline of. The same root gives shakl, "shape," a word many Hindi speakers also use.
So "difficult" in Hindi is not "heavy" or "hard" but "hard to make out." That is a different metaphor from the English one, and worth carrying with you.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: which adjectives bend, and why

utterances: adjective: काला. origin: Sanskrit, ends in -आ. changes ending?: yes.
adjective: सफ़ेद. origin: Persian loan. changes ending?: no.
adjective: आसान. origin: Persian loan. changes ending?: no.
adjective: मुश्किल. origin: Arabic loan. changes ending?: no.

segments.text: There is a pattern under this, and it is about shape rather than about borrowing. A Hindi adjective bends when it ends in -आ; otherwise it stays put. Loanwords land on the "no" side so often because they mostly arrive ending in a consonant.
That means you do not have to remember a list. Look at the ending.

segments.text: What shape does a Hindi adjective need before it will bend? (An ending in -आ.) What is the literal idea inside मुश्किल? (Something whose shape is unclear — from the Arabic root for form.)

lessons.title: सुंदर / बदसूरत (sundar / badsūrat) — beautiful, ugly, and a prefix you already own
lessons.gloss: beautiful and ugly — a prefix you have already met, and a face

segments.text: You met सुप्रभात as "good morning." Say it again and listen to the first syllable. You are about to meet it a second time, in a word that has nothing to do with mornings.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: सुंदर and बदसूरत

segments.text: Neither ends in -आ, so neither bends. You can put both to work with what you learned last lesson and nothing else.

सुंदर opens with Sanskrit सु- — the prefix meaning "good, well." It is the same सु- sitting at the front of सुप्रभात ("good dawn"). Once you have noticed it, you will keep finding it: सु- marks the favourable version of whatever follows.
बदसूरत is two borrowings glued together. बद is Persian for "bad," and सूरत is Arabic ṣūrat, "face" or "form." Ugly, in Hindi, is literally "bad-faced."

बद and English bad look like the same word and are not related. The resemblance is one of the most famous coincidences in etymology — two unconnected languages landing on nearly the same sound for nearly the same meaning. Enjoy it, and do not build a rule on it.

So the pair is built from opposite halves of Hindi's vocabulary: सुंदर is Sanskrit through and through, बदसूरत is Persian plus Arabic. The language names beauty with its inherited words and ugliness with its borrowed ones, which is an accident of history rather than a judgement, but it is a useful one to notice — it tells you which dictionary each word's relatives live in.

segments.instruction: which of the four adjectives you now have would change ending in front of a feminine noun (none of them — not one ends in -आ)

segments.text: Where have you seen सु- before this lesson, and what does it do? (In सुप्रभात — it marks the good version of what follows.) What are the two pieces of बदसूरत, and what do they add up to? (Persian बद "bad" plus Arabic सूरत "face" — bad-faced.)
